# Step 2: Understand the System, Structure, Component(s)

This step builds a clear, practical understanding of the system being
assessed, in the context of climate change. Teams should review how the
system is designed, built, operated, maintained, and how it influences
other systems to deliver its intended service. This understanding helps
the assessment stay focused on the parts of the systems that matter most
for safety, performance, and continuity, and it provides the system
information needed to assess climate hazards and exposure. The level of
detail should match the scope and objective confirmed previously. For a
simple assessment, the system may be a single component. For a
system-wide or higher-risk assessment, the system may include multiple
critical structures, components, sub-components, and supporting
services.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-align: center
%%| fig-cap: "Generic Workflow for Adaptation"
---
config:
    flowchart:
        curve: linear
---
flowchart-elk TD
    A[Step 1: Develop Scope]:::basic --> B[Step 2: Understand System]:::focus
    B --> C[Step 3: Hazard & Exposure Assessment]:::basic
    C --> D[Step 4: Vulnerability Assessment]:::basic
    H[Step 7: Institutionalize Decision]:::basic
    D --> |No Vulnerability| H
    D --> |Vulnerable| E[Step 5: Risk Assessment]:::basic
    F[Step 6: Adaptation Plan]:::basic
    D & E --- J1[ ]:::join
    J1 --> |Unacceptable Vulnerability or Risk| F
    E --> |Risk Acceptable| H
    F --> H

    classDef basic fill:#CAD4D6
    classDef focus fill:#CE153D
    classDef join height:0px
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Inputs"}
Typical inputs for this step include engineering drawings and design
basis information, system specifications, operating procedures,
maintenance strategies, condition and inspection reports, operational
experience, and prior risk or event documentation (such as near misses).
:::


Actions for this step may include reviewing the available documentation,
walking down the system where practical, and engaging station staff and
subject matter experts (SMEs) to confirm how it works in practice, how
it is maintained, what has changed since installation, and what current
condition and age imply for performance. This step also includes
checking for "design intent versus current reality" and avoiding
assumptions that aging systems will continue to perform as originally
specified, even in the face of a changing climate.


::: {.callout collapse="true" title="Outcomes"}

Outcomes of this step may include:

-   Documented understanding of the system and how it works with other
    systems to deliver its intended service, written at a level of
    detail that fits the assessment scope and decision need
-   List of systems, structures and components critical aspects that
    will be included in the assessment
-   For each critical aspect identified for the system, the output
    typically captures key specifications, known condition issues,
    relevant operating experience (OPEX) or reports, and SME insights.
    This step may also produce a preliminary view of climate sensitivity
    by identifying design and operating thresholds linked to
    meteorological or climate indicators (e.g., precipitation
    intensities, flood levels, wind speeds, temperature operating
    ranges, icing conditions, or low-water constraints). Staff "lived
    experience" is often a useful input at this stage, especially where
    performance changes or operational challenges have been observed
    during past weather events.
:::
